intro_en:
The Israel National Trail crosses Makhtesh Ramon (the Ramon Crater) – the largest of all the Negev craters, about 40 km long. The crossing of the crater, from Mitzpe Ramon to Shen Ramon, is made at its center – at its relatively narrow "waist", about 8 km wide. Along the way we encounter unique geological phenomena exposed in the crater and its surroundings.

 Nahal Hava – Mitzpe Ramon (42)
 Nahal Gevanim – Gev Holit (44)
character_en: A slightly steep descent into the crater, and two steep climbs to Shen Ramon and to Spot Height 660 (the second climb can be bypassed). The rest of the route follows an easy walking line.
shortcuts_en: The segment can be shortened by descending into the crater from Mitzpe Ramon on the green trail, skipping the loop via Har Gamal and the field school. Another shortcut option is to end the walk at Road 40, after the Ammonite Wall.
transport_en: At the starting point in Mitzpe Ramon
important_en: Drinking water and an organized campsite are available at the Be'erot campsite, about 3 km of walking on an easy track from the Nahal Gevanim overnight campsite.
In Mitzpe Ramon, not far from the trail, there is a supermarket, cafes and restaurants.
description_en:
We return to the Israel National Trail at the access road to the Beresheet Hotel. The trail passes between the hotel's access road and the Mitzpe Ramon–Eilat road (Road 40).
We cross Road 40 on a pedestrian bridge leading to the visitors' center. For those interested, the center offers an overview and preliminary introduction to Makhtesh Ramon before crossing it. Entrance fee.
From the visitors' center, the trail proceeds along the crater rim, passing several lookout points over the crater's expanses and surroundings. To the right, the southern neighborhood of Mitzpe Ramon.
Mitzpe Ramon was founded in the 1950s, during the paving of the first road to Eilat through the Negev (Road 40), and against the background of the development of clay and gypsum mines in Makhtesh Ramon. The town's development slowed after another road to Eilat was paved, the Arava road (Road 90), which took precedence and became the main route to the southern city. Today about 6,000 residents live in Mitzpe Ramon. Initiatives in tourism, art and education introduced here in recent years have contributed to population growth and human diversity.
Note: in line with the last residential building on the town street to the right, a green-marked trail crosses the Israel National Trail. The green trail descends into the crater and offers a shortcut for those interested – to descend into the crater earlier and skip the loop via Har Gamal and the field school.
The Israel National Trail continues with a black marking, proceeding along the crater rim to Har Gamal (Camel Mountain). Har Gamal is an environmental sculpture created by nature, in the shape of a kneeling camel – that is, a camel made to sit down on its knees – overlooking the crater. An observation deck was built on the camel's hump, from which one can look in every direction, to the west of the crater and north to Mitzpe Ramon and its surroundings.
Har Gamal stands 892 meters high – one of the highest points on the Israel National Trail. On its way from the north, the trail passed a high point on Mount Amasa in the southern Hebron Hills – at 850 meters – and from there descended to minus 390 meters at the Dead Sea. From Mitzpe Ramon southward, the Israel National Trail continues on a descending trend, down to sea level at Sapir in the Arava. From the Arava, the trail climbs to 750 meters, between Shaharut and Be'er Milhan.
A short distance from Har Gamal, the trail enters the compound of the Har HaNegev Field School. Here there is water and toilets and a recommended lodging option. We pass through a gate in the fence, and the exit for the descent is through another gate, on the far side of a large observation terrace.
The Israel National Trail descends into the crater along a gentle spur, with a blue-marked trail. Opposite is the crater's southern wall – which is not continuous and complete, unlike the northern craters – the Small and the Large Makhtesh. The gap where the continuity of the crater wall is broken is called the Pitam Gap, after Mount Pitam, which lies nearby outside the crater. Makhtesh Ramon is a "worn" crater. Since it was formed, geological events have damaged its perfect crater shape; fractures and faults have altered the order and continuity of geological layers and structures, within it and around it.
At the end of the descent, the trail enters the channel of Nahal Ramon for a relatively short distance. Nahal Ramon drains almost the entire area of the crater, apart from the Ardon Valley, and carries away the material produced by the weathering and erosion processes that create the crater. The stream breaks out of the crater at Sha'ar Ramon (Ramon Gate). Up to this point it has drained the area of the crater to the west, from the corner of the crater at the foot of Mount Ramon, near the border with Egypt. That is a distance of about 20 km westward and an area of about 60 sq km.
A green strip of white broom bushes and other plants accompanies the line of the channel. In the channel wall a layer of Jurassic sandstone is exposed, one of the deepest and oldest layers exposed in the crater floor.
Note: after a short walk in the channel of Nahal Ramon, the Israel National Trail changes direction. The trail leaves the Nahal Ramon channel and climbs gently north toward the northern crater wall. Those who wish can continue walking in the Nahal Ramon channel with a black-marked trail, shortening the route but giving up the "Prism Wall". After about 2.5 km they meet the Israel National Trail again.
After turning out of the Nahal Ramon channel, the Israel National Trail continues to the junction with a green-marked trail descending from the crater wall (the one used by those who chose the shortcut from Mitzpe Ramon).
The trail turns right, with the green marking, passes to the left of and at the foot of a dark hill, enters a channel and proceeds to a dark outcrop in the channel wall known as the "Prism Wall". This is evidence of ancient "baking" processes deep in the earth – heating and cooling of sand and rocks that created the prisms. It is a phenomenon similar to the familiar hexagons of the Golan Heights.
Near the prisms, the Israel National Trail turns left, toward the south-east, together with a red marking. The trail proceeds down a sandy channel and reaches Nahal Ramon together with it.
Immediately after crossing Nahal Ramon stands a broad-crowned acacia tree, inviting a rest stop in its shade.
The walk continues in the same direction on a red-marked dirt road. After a short distance, a dark, pointed peak appears from time to time on the skyline – Shen Ramon (Ramon's Tooth). On the way to Shen Ramon, we cross an area where the oldest rocks in the crater are exposed – limestone and gypsum rocks formed more than 200 million years ago, in the Triassic period.
At a trail junction, the Israel National Trail leaves the dirt road, turns right and continues with the red marking. We climb gently over a pale surface, which takes on darker hues as we approach the dark mass of Shen Ramon.
Shen Ramon is a magmatic mountain. In an ancient period, magmatic material erupted from deep in the earth and intruded between the layers of marine sedimentary rocks. The magma cooled slowly and crystallized into a pocket of igneous rock – which was exposed at the surface during the formation of the crater.
The climb continues inside a channel toward the dark mountain. The climb begins gently and gradually becomes steep up to the summit of the "Tooth", at 698 meters. From here there is a 360-degree view into the crater and beyond it. One can see the dip of the layers in the southern crater wall, which looks close, on both sides of the Shen Ramon summit.
Outside the crater, among the pale hills, there is a green strip. This is Nahal Nekarot, which flows parallel to the crater's southern wall. It rises south of Mount Arod in the west of the crater, and empties into Nahal HaArava near Moshav Ein Yahav.
On the other side of the summit, the trail descends steeply on its way out of the crater. One can make out the clear boundary line the trail crosses, in the transition from the dark rock of Shen Ramon to the pale rocks – the sedimentary rocks that form the ribs of the crater wall. This is the line of an ancient fault that the magma from which the Shen Ramon rock formed "exploited" in order to break through and intrude between the layers of sedimentary rock.
In the area where the trail enters among the ribs, we bypass a dry waterfall and a rock pool (gev). The trail completes the descent and approaches the channel of Nahal Nekarot, but a little before that it turns left, toward the north-east, toward the "Ammonite Wall". At the turning point a lone acacia tree can be seen on the right, standing close to the trail. It is a pleasant shady spot for a break.
The Israel National Trail proceeds for a stretch parallel to and at the foot of the ribs of the crater wall. At the point where the trail hugs the base of the ribs, a sloping wall can be seen to the left of the trail – the "Ammonite Wall".
Ammonites are ancient marine creatures that lived millions of years ago and became extinct in the same period as the dinosaurs. Here too, the crater and its surroundings offer a glimpse of ancient geological events. The ammonites fossilized on the floor of the sea in which they lived, leaving traces of their existence to this day. If you look closely at the sloping surface, you can make out round spiral fossils. The diameter of a fossilized ammonite can reach that of a basketball.
We continue with the trail to a Y-shaped fork; the Israel National Trail turns left with a green marking and climbs steeply to Spot Height 660, a peak at the top of the ribs with a fine view over the crater and its surroundings.
Those who wish to skip the effort of the climb can bypass the mountain. At the Y-shaped fork, turn right and continue with the red marking toward Road 40. Here the whole segment can be shortened and the walk ended. Alternatively, a short distance before the road, turn left onto a black-marked trail and walk parallel to Road 40 until meeting the Israel National Trail.
Those who choose to climb to Spot Height 660, with the Israel National Trail and the green-marked trail, ascend a channel that passes between the ribs and climbs steeply to the ridgeline. Here a fine view opens up to the center of the crater. One can identify Shen Ramon to the left, Mitzpe Ramon opposite, and to the right Givat Ga'ash, Ma'ale Mahmal, the Mahmal Valley, Mount Ardon and the Ardon Valley.
On the descent from Spot Height 660 to Road 40, toward the end of the descent and to the left of the trail, one can identify the Gevanim Valley. In the valley there are dark rock masses – "humps" – relatively small magmatic intrusions that crystallized between pale sedimentary rocks. In other words, a geological process similar to Shen Ramon – but in miniature.
We cross Road 40 carefully and walk parallel to the road to a dirt road that leaves it eastward, in the channel of Nahal Gevanim. The road leads to the Nahal Gevanim overnight campsite, next to the junction with the Oil Road (Tzir HaNeft), at the foot of Mount Saharonim.
Points of interest: the visitors' center in Mitzpe Ramon (entrance fee), the crater promenade. Har Gamal, 892 meters high – one of the highest points on the Israel National Trail. "The Prisms" – a unique geological phenomenon. Shen Ramon – a mountain of magma. The Ammonite Wall – fossils millions of years old. Spot Height 660 – a peak at the top of the ribs of Makhtesh Ramon.
